title: Hindi for children | Online lessons with Neelam
description: Begin with familiar words, playful questions and everyday conversation. Help your child make Hindi a language they can use, not just a list of words to memorise.
lead: Begin with familiar words, playful questions and everyday conversation. Help your child make Hindi a language they can use, not just a list of words to memorise.

sections.title: Start with what your child already knows
sections.body: A child who understands a grandparent has a different starting point from a complete beginner. Tell Neelam what your child hears at home, what they can say comfortably, and whether they have encountered Devanagari. The first conversation helps identify a suitable learning focus.

sections.title: Make speaking feel safe
sections.body: Begin with greetings, colours, favourite foods and family names. Model a short sentence, give time to respond, and accept an imperfect attempt. Reading, writing and longer conversations can follow as confidence develops.

sections.title: Your role at home
sections.body: A familiar adult can help a younger learner settle into an online session. Between lessons, choose one small routine: a Hindi greeting at breakfast, naming three things in a room, or asking a grandparent a question. Practise without turning every conversation into a correction.

sections.title: Discuss the right fit
sections.body: Age, attention span, language exposure and family goals all matter. Enquire about a suitable format and lesson length before booking. Fees, age suitability and available times are confirmed individually; this page does not promise a fixed timetable.

heading: Hindi for children

title: Hindi for heritage learners | Online lessons with Neelam
description: For families where Hindi is heard at home, but English is the easier answer. Build a bridge between familiar sounds and confident conversation.
lead: For families where Hindi is heard at home, but English is the easier answer. Build a bridge between familiar sounds and confident conversation.

sections.title: Understanding and speaking are different skills
sections.body: A learner may follow a family conversation without having the words ready to reply. Start with a topic they already understand, then practise short responses. Being bilingual does not require equal ability in every language or every situation.

sections.title: Give the conversation a real purpose
sections.body: Choose something worth saying: asking what is for dinner, telling a grandparent about a favourite game, or sharing a small story from school. Use a sentence frame, then change one word at a time. Familiarity reduces the effort needed to start.

sections.title: Keep identity and language separate
sections.body: A child does not need to prove their identity by speaking perfectly. Avoid comparing siblings or insisting on Hindi during an emotional conversation. Invite participation, allow English support, and recognise attempts as progress.

sections.title: Bring your family’s Hindi
sections.body: Families use different words, pronunciations and combinations of languages. Tell Neelam which expressions are familiar at home. Reading and writing can be a separate goal, rather than a prerequisite for speaking.

heading: Hindi for heritage learners

title: Hindi for beginners | Online lessons with Neelam
description: Build a foundation in everyday Hindi: introductions, useful questions and the sounds behind the words. Ask about a learning plan for your age and goals.
lead: Build a foundation in everyday Hindi: introductions, useful questions and the sounds behind the words. Ask about a learning plan for your age and goals.

sections.title: Begin with useful phrases
sections.body: Namaste is a useful greeting. Aap kaise hain? asks “How are you?” respectfully. Learn the meaning, listen to the sound with a teacher, and practise using a phrase in an actual exchange instead of repeating it in isolation.

sections.title: Connect words into a sentence
sections.body: A sentence frame such as Mera naam … hai (“My name is …”) lets you introduce yourself. Notice what stays the same and what changes. A small set of reusable patterns is more useful than a long vocabulary list without context.

sections.title: Use transliteration as a bridge
sections.body: Roman letters can help you begin, but they do not represent every Hindi sound precisely. Ask for feedback on pronunciation. Devanagari can be introduced alongside conversation when it matches your goals.

sections.title: Tell us what you want to do
sections.body: Family conversations, a visit to India and reading simple words need different practice. Adult learners should ask Neelam about current availability and suitability. No particular age range or adult course schedule is guaranteed here.

title: Hindi reading and writing | Online lessons with Neelam
description: Explore Devanagari at a manageable pace, connecting familiar spoken Hindi with vowels, consonants and simple written words.
lead: Explore Devanagari at a manageable pace, connecting familiar spoken Hindi with vowels, consonants and simple written words.

sections.title: Meet the script
sections.body: Hindi is commonly written in Devanagari. Begin by distinguishing a few letters visually and connecting each with a sound. A learner who already speaks some Hindi can use familiar words to make that connection more meaningful.

sections.title: Understand vowels and matras
sections.body: Independent vowels are used when a vowel begins a syllable without a preceding consonant. Dependent vowel signs, called matras, combine with consonants. For example, क with ा becomes का. Learn a small set accurately before adding more.

sections.title: Read before copying long passages
sections.body: Match a sound to a letter, recognise it in a short word, and then try writing it. Large, comfortable letter shapes can be easier for a beginner than dense worksheets. Handwriting is one part of literacy, not the only measure of understanding.

sections.title: Agree a starting point
sections.body: Tell Neelam whether the learner recognises letters, reads short words or needs a complete introduction. Our vowel sheet is a starting sample, not a complete Hindi alphabet or a replacement for pronunciation guidance.

heading: Hindi reading and writing

description: Start with Hindi vowel practice, family phrases and a five-minute routine. Free beginner-friendly resources for families.
lead: Small, useful things to try together. Start with a greeting, notice a letter, and make room for a little Hindi in your day.

sections.title: Choose one starting point
sections.body: You do not need to work through everything at once. Pick a resource that matches your learner: family phrases for speaking, vowels for reading, or a five-minute routine to make practice feel manageable.

heading: A little Hindi, every day.

title: Hindi vowels for beginners | Devanagari practice
description: Learn a starter set of Hindi vowels with Devanagari, transliteration and a printable practice sheet.
lead: A small first step into Devanagari. Notice the shape, say the sound with a teacher, then practise one letter at a time.

sections.title: How to use this starter sheet
sections.body: This is a starter set of common independent vowels, not a full account of Hindi spelling or pronunciation. Roman spellings are approximate. Read the letter with a teacher, trace its shape with your finger, then write it on paper.

sections.title: From an independent vowel to a matra
sections.body: आ is an independent vowel. Its dependent sign ा can attach to a consonant: क + ा = का. Compare the full vowel with the smaller sign. This distinction is useful before moving to longer words.

sections.title: Try a two-minute practice
sections.body: Choose अ and आ. Point to each, say its sound, and notice which lasts longer. Then cover the transliteration and recognise the letters again. Stop while the activity still feels comfortable.

heading: Meet the Hindi vowels.

title: Hindi phrases for family conversations | Beginner guide
description: Practise respectful Hindi greetings, introductions and questions for speaking with family. Includes Devanagari and transliteration.
lead: A few words can make a family conversation feel closer. Try one greeting and one question in your next call.

sections.title: Use respectful forms with elders
sections.body: Aap is a respectful way to say “you”. Aap kaise hain? is a useful greeting to practise with grandparents or other elders. Your family may use different expressions; ask which sounds most natural to them.

sections.title: Make space for a reply
sections.body: After asking a question, wait and listen. You can repeat a familiar word or answer partly in English while you learn. The goal is a genuine exchange, not a perfect performance.

sections.title: Build your own family phrasebook
sections.body: Write down one phrase a relative actually uses, ask what it means, and try using it the next time. Personal words can be more memorable than a large generic list.

heading: Words that bring us closer.

title: A five-minute Hindi routine for children | Parent guide
description: A practical five-minute Hindi routine with listening, speaking and playful recall for families abroad.
lead: A short routine is easier to return to. Try five calm minutes together, with room for mistakes and plenty of familiar words.

sections.title: Minute 1 · Listen
sections.body: Choose three familiar objects or a photograph. Say their Hindi names slowly and point to them. Let the learner listen before asking for a response.

sections.title: Minute 2 · Choose
sections.body: Offer a choice between two objects. Ask the learner to point, then model the word again. Recognition can come before speaking.

sections.title: Minute 3 · Say
sections.body: Invite a word or a short sentence. Accept a small attempt and model a natural reply. Avoid interrupting every sound with a correction.

sections.title: Minute 4 · Change one thing
sections.body: Swap an object, a colour or a person in the phrase. The familiar pattern helps the new word feel less daunting.

sections.title: Minute 5 · Connect
sections.body: Use the phrase for a real purpose: greet someone, describe a snack, or ask a family member a question. Stop here and return another day rather than stretching the activity until it becomes tiring.

heading: Five minutes. One small connection.

title: Hindi alphabet for beginners | Devanagari letters and sounds
description: Explore Hindi vowels, consonant groups, matras and common letter combinations. A clear Devanagari reference for children and beginner learners.
lead: Meet the building blocks of written Hindi. Use this reference a little at a time, with spoken guidance to connect each shape to its sound.
heading: A first map of the Hindi alphabet.

sections.title: Letters belong to a system
sections.body: Hindi is usually written in Devanagari. Consonant letters normally include an inherent vowel sound; vowel signs and other marks change how they are read. The groups below are a practical reference, not a promise that pronunciation can be learned from English spelling alone.

sections.title: Start with a few familiar sounds
sections.body: Look at two or three letters at a time. Ask a teacher to model each sound, recognise the letter in a familiar word, then try writing it. The consonant groups reflect how sounds are made, so letters that look related are not always the ones that sound alike.

sections.title: Independent vowels and vowel signs
sections.body: आ can stand as an independent vowel, while ा attaches to a consonant: क + ा = का. Similarly, क + ि = कि and क + ी = की. The sign ि is written to the left of the consonant but pronounced after it. अं and अः are commonly taught alongside vowels, but they use additional marks; they are not both simple independent vowel letters.

sections.title: Additional forms and joined letters
sections.body: Hindi also uses forms such as ड़, ढ़, क़, ख़, ग़, ज़ and फ़. A dot called a nukta distinguishes these from their base letters. क्ष, त्र and ज्ञ are familiar letter combinations, not three additional single consonants. Different teaching charts count letters differently because they include or separate such forms.

sections.title: A small activity for today
sections.body: Find आ, क and म in the reference. Compare क with का. Then ask a teacher to model a familiar word such as आम (mango). Recognising a word you already know can help connect written shapes with meaning.
